14.lecture_title: Company Law: Liability for Misstatement in Prospectus
14.memory_hook: Think of a prospectus as a corporate dating profile: if you lie about your assets and liabilities to lure investors into a commitment, you will be sued for damages and fraud.
14.concept_explanation:
A prospectus is the invitation by which a public company asks the public to invest their hard-earned money by subscribing to its shares or debentures. Because investors rely entirely on the representations made in this document before parting with their capital, the law imposes the strictest standards of honesty on its makers. When a statement in a prospectus is misleading, deceptive, or conceals a vital material fact, it is classified as a misstatement. Under the Companies Act, 2013, those who authorized the prospectus cannot hide behind corporate veils; liability is personal, piercing through directors, promoters, and experts.

Liability for misstatements is broadly divided into two categories: civil liability and criminal liability. Civil liability focuses on compensating the investor who suffered financial loss because they acted on the faith of the false prospectus. Under Section 35, the company and every director, promoter, or person who authorized the issue can be sued for damages by any person who sustained loss or damage. Conversely, criminal liability under Section 34 targets the moral wrong and fraud, punishing the perpetrators with imprisonment and fines. The underlying philosophy is caveat vendor—let the seller beware—shifting the burden of verification entirely onto the company and its managers.

To establish liability, an aggrieved investor does not need to prove fraudulent intent for civil damages, though it helps; proving that a material statement was false or misleading and that they acted upon it to their detriment is sufficient. However, the law provides statutory defences under Section 35(2). For instance, a director can escape liability if they withdrew their consent before the issue, or if the prospectus was issued without their knowledge or consent and they gave reasonable public notice thereof once they came to know of it. Understanding these boundaries separates a negligent manager from a fraudulent conspirator.
key_provisions: Section 34 — Criminal liability for misstatements in prospectus, punishable with imprisonment under Section 447.
Section 35 — Civil liability for persons who sustain loss or damage due to inclusion of misleading statements or omission of material facts.
Section 36 — Punishment for fraudulently inducing persons to invest money through misleading, false, or deceptive statements.
Section 38 — Punishment for fraudulently procuring persons to subscribe for shares in a company under fictitious names.

case_laws.case_name: Derry v. Peek
case_laws.facts: A tramway company issued a prospectus stating that they had the right to use steam power instead of horses, assuming the Board of Trade's permission was a mere formality. Later, the Board refused permission, and the company wound up; the plaintiff, who bought shares relying on this statement, sued for deceit.
case_laws.holding: The House of Lords held that fraud is proved when it is shown that a false representation has been made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly careless whether it be true or false. Honest belief in the truth of the statement, even if foolish or negligent, absolves a defendant from an action for deceit.
case_laws.why_it_matters: This landmark case established the classic definition of common law deceit and proved inadequate for modern investor protection, prompting legislatures to enact strict statutory liabilities that do not require proof of intentional fraud.

case_laws.case_name: Peek v. Gurney
case_laws.facts: A prospectus was issued containing fraudulent suppressions of material facts regarding the company's financial health. The plaintiff did not buy shares on the original allotment but purchased them later on the open market, subsequently suffering heavy losses.
case_laws.holding: The House of Lords held that the function of a prospectus is exhausted once the shares are allotted to the original applicants. Subsequent purchasers on the secondary market cannot sue the directors for misstatements in the original prospectus unless they can show a direct link.
case_laws.why_it_matters: Clarified the crucial limitation that a prospectus's protective ambit extends only to the original allottees who subscribed on the faith of it, restricting remote claims.

14.real_world_example: When major startups or established firms fudge their growth metrics, user numbers, or debt profiles in their initial public offering (IPO) red herring prospectuses to attract high valuations from retail and institutional investors, regulatory bodies like SEBI step in. Investors who bought shares at listing only to see values crash upon truth discovery file class-action suits seeking full restitution under civil liability provisions.
14.illustration: Company X issues a prospectus for a public issue stating that it owns prime commercial real estate worth 50 crores free of encumbrances. In reality, the land is heavily mortgaged to a bank, and directors knew this but omitted the detail. Investor A reads the prospectus, applies for shares, and suffers a 2-lakh loss when the truth emerges and share prices collapse. Under Section 35, Investor A can sue the directors personally for compensation, and the directors cannot claim they made an honest mistake because omitting a mortgage is a material concealment.
14.quick_answer: Liability for misstatement in a prospectus arises when a statement is untrue, misleading, or a material fact is omitted, inducing an investor to buy shares and suffer loss. Under the Companies Act, 2013, this liability is dual: Civil (Section 35) and Criminal (Section 34). Civil liability makes the company, directors, promoters, and experts jointly and severally liable to pay compensation for damages to any person who sustained loss. Criminal liability punishes fraud with imprisonment under Section 447. Statutory defences are available to directors under Section 35(2) if they prove they withdrew consent, or that the prospectus was issued without their knowledge and they gave immediate public notice. Key landmark cases include Derry v. Peek, which established that honest belief negates common law deceit, leading to stricter statutory duties today.
14.essay_answer:
Introduction: A prospectus is the cornerstone of corporate capitalization, serving as an invitation to the public to invest. Because investors rely entirely on its disclosures, the law mandates absolute fidelity. When a prospectus contains untrue statements or suppresses material facts, it constitutes a misstatement, triggering severe legal consequences under the Companies Act, 2013.

Civil Liability under Section 35: Section 35 provides that where a person has subscribed for securities of a company acting on a prospectus containing a misleading statement or omission, the company and every person who is a director, promoter, or named as a director at the time of the issue shall be liable to pay compensation to every such person for any loss or damage sustained. Unlike common law deceit which required proof of fraud, Section 35 holds managers accountable for negligence and misrepresentation unless specific statutory defences are proved. These defences include withdrawing consent in writing before the issue or proving that the prospectus was issued without the director's knowledge or consent and reasonable public notice was given.

Criminal Liability under Section 34: Where a prospectus includes any statement which is untrue or misleading in form or context in which it is included, or where any inclusion or omission of matter is made with an intent to mislead, every person who authorized the issue of such prospectus shall be punishable under Section 447 for fraud. This carries mandatory prison terms, emphasizing that corporate deception is a serious criminal offence against society.

Judicial Interpretation and Limitations: Landmark jurisprudence has shaped these principles. In Derry v. Peek, the House of Lords held that honest belief in a statement, however foolish, negates deceit, highlighting the gap that modern statutory provisions now fill. Furthermore, Peek v. Gurney established that the prospectus's life ends with the original allotment, barring secondary market purchasers from suing under it.

Conclusion: Liability for misstatements protects market integrity. By imposing personal civil and criminal burdens on directors and promoters, the law ensures that corporate growth is fueled by transparent truth rather than deceptive promises.
14.exam_angle: Examiners frequently test this topic through comprehensive problem-based practical questions where a director claims they were unaware of an omission made by an accountant. To score top marks, clearly distinguish between civil liability (Section 35) and criminal liability (Section 34), discuss the statutory defences available, and weave in case laws like Derry v. Peek to show historical context.
quick_recap: Prospectus misstatement = untrue statement or material omission.
Section 35 deals with civil liability (compensation for loss).
Section 34 deals with criminal liability (fraud/imprisonment).
Statutory defences: withdrawal of consent or lack of knowledge with public notice.
Derry v. Peek: honest belief rules out common law deceit.
Peek v. Gurney: prospectus remedy limited to original allottees.
14.importance_reason: This is a core Unit II topic that routinely appears as both a direct essay question and a practical problem-solving scenario in university exams.

15.topic: Civil, Criminal Liability and Compounding of Offences
15.lecture_title: Civil, Criminal Liability and Compounding of Offences under the Companies Act, 2013
15.memory_hook: Civil liability is about paying back the damage from your pocket, criminal liability is about doing time for your fraud, and compounding is paying the government to wipe the slate clean before it goes to trial.
15.concept_explanation:
When a company acts, it does so through human agency—its directors, key managerial personnel, and officers in default. Under the Companies Act, 2013, when things go wrong, accountability is split into two distinct categories: civil liability and criminal liability, alongside a procedural mechanism known as compounding of offences.

Civil liability arises primarily from breaches of statutory duties, misstatements in a prospectus, or fraud causing financial loss to investors or creditors. The core remedy here is compensatory and restitutional—meaning the wrongdoer must pay damages, restore losses, or make good the financial injury caused. Provisions like Section 35 of the Act make directors personally liable for losses suffered by those who subscribed to securities based on misleading prospectuses.

Criminal liability, on the other hand, involves penal consequences such as fines, imprisonment, or both, designed to punish intentional wrongdoing, systemic non-compliance, fraud, or failure to adhere to mandatory disclosures. Sections 447, 134, and 448 deal with serious offenses like fraud, false statements, and non-compliance with reporting standards. Importantly, the Act introduces the concept of an 'officer who is in default' to ensure that liability falls specifically on those responsible for managing the compliance failure rather than every single board member.

To prevent the criminal justice system from collapsing under the weight of thousands of technical or procedural defaults, the Act provides for compounding of offences under Section 441. Compounding is a settlement mechanism where, for offences punishable with fine only, or fine and imprisonment where imprisonment is not mandatory, the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) or Regional Director permits the offender to pay a compounding fee instead of undergoing prosecution. This balances regulatory enforcement with ease of doing business.
key_provisions: Section 35 — Civil liability for misstatements in prospectus
Section 134 — Penalty for failure to attach financial statements and board reports
Section 441 — Compounding of certain offences
Section 447 — Punishment for fraud
Section 448 — Punishment for false statements

case_laws.case_name: Standard Chartered Bank v. Directorate of Enforcement
case_laws.facts: The appellant bank faced prosecution for alleged violations under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA), where the statute prescribed mandatory imprisonment alongside a fine. The question arose whether a corporate body, being a juristic person incapable of physical imprisonment, could be prosecuted for offenses requiring mandatory imprisonment.
case_laws.holding: The Supreme Court held that a company can be prosecuted and fined even for offenses where the statute prescribes a mandatory sentence of imprisonment, as the court can impose the fine while ignoring the imprisonment part for a juristic entity.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It established the modern precedent that corporations are criminally liable and cannot escape prosecution merely because they cannot be physically imprisoned.

case_laws.case_name: V.L.S. Finance Ltd. v. Union of India
case_laws.facts: A challenge was brought regarding the constitutionality and scope of compounding of offenses under the Companies Act, questioning whether compounding could occur before or after the initiation of criminal proceedings.
case_laws.holding: The Supreme Court held that compounding under Section 441 can be done either before or after the institution of any prosecution, providing a wide window for corporate offenders to settle compoundable offenses.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It cemented compounding as an effective statutory mechanism to decongest courts and encourage voluntary compliance.

15.real_world_example: When major corporate governance failures occur—such as the massive financial misstatements uncovered in companies like Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services (IL&FS)—investigative agencies step in. The Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) initiates criminal prosecutions under Section 447 for fraud, while affected institutional investors and debenture holders file civil suits seeking recovery of lost capital. Simultaneously, smaller firms caught in procedural delays apply for compounding of offenses to clear their compliance records before listing on stock exchanges.
15.illustration: Alpha Tech Ltd. files a prospectus containing material misstatements to lure public investors. Investor X suffers a loss of Rs. 5 lakhs. Simultaneously, the company fails to file its annual returns within the statutory deadline, a technical default. Under civil law, Investor X can sue the directors under Section 35 for compensation. For the technical filing default, Alpha Tech can apply for compounding under Section 441 by paying the prescribed fee to the NCLT. However, for the fraudulent misstatements, the directors face criminal prosecution under Section 447, which cannot be compounded if it involves public interest or non-compoundable categories.
15.quick_answer: Civil liability in company law focuses on compensating victims for financial losses caused by breaches of statutory duties, such as misstatements in a prospectus under Section 35. Criminal liability, governed by provisions like Section 447 for fraud, imposes penal consequences including fines and imprisonment on officers in default. Since not all corporate defaults warrant severe penal action, Section 441 provides for compounding of offences—a statutory mechanism allowing companies and officers to pay a compounding fee to the NCLT or Regional Director to settle compoundable offenses and avoid prolonged criminal trial. This dual framework ensures investor protection and corporate accountability while maintaining judicial efficiency.
15.essay_answer:
Introduction: Corporate entities operate as legal persons driven by human agency. To regulate this dynamic, the Companies Act, 2013 establishes a robust framework of corporate accountability categorized into civil liability, criminal liability, and the mechanism of compounding of offences. This tripartite division ensures that wrongs against individuals or investors are adequately compensated, heinous economic crimes are severely punished, and minor technical defaults are efficiently resolved without clogging the criminal justice system.

Civil Liability: Civil liability is remedial and compensatory in nature. It is triggered when a breach of statutory duty inflicts specific financial loss upon investors, creditors, or the company itself. A prime example is Section 35 of the Companies Act, which imposes personal civil liability on directors, promoters, and experts for any loss or damage sustained by subscribers who relied on a misleading or fraudulent prospectus. Unlike criminal law, the standard of proof is based on a preponderance of probabilities, and the primary objective is to restore the injured party to their original financial position through damages.

Criminal Liability and the Concept of 'Officer in Default': Criminal liability penalizes intentional wrongdoing, fraud, and severe non-compliance. Section 447 is the cornerstone of criminal provisions under the 2013 Act, prescribing rigorous imprisonment and hefty fines for fraud involving public interest or specified monetary thresholds. To prevent unjust targeting of non-executive or independent directors, the Act introduces the concept of 'officer who is in default' under Section 2(60), pinning liability on managing directors, whole-time directors, CFOs, CSs, and specific designated officers responsible for compliance.

Compounding of Offences: Recognizing that criminal trials are time-consuming and that many corporate defaults are technical or inadvertent, Section 441 provides for the compounding of offences. Offenses punishable only with fine, or with fine and imprisonment (where imprisonment is discretionary), can be compounded by the NCLT or Regional Director upon payment of the requisite sum. As affirmed in judicial precedents like V.L.S. Finance, compounding can occur either before or after the institution of prosecution, serving as a vital tool for corporate remediation.

Conclusion: The interplay between civil and criminal liability, balanced by the safety valve of compounding, forms the bedrock of modern corporate jurisprudence in India. It deters malfeasance, safeguards stakeholder investments, and maintains regulatory compliance without paralyzing the ease of doing business.
15.exam_angle: Examiners frequently test this topic through problem-based questions where a director commits a statutory default and a fraudulent misstatement simultaneously. To score high, clearly separate the civil remedies available to investors from the criminal prosecution pathways and discuss whether the specific default is compoundable under Section 441.
quick_recap: Civil liability = compensatory, aimed at recovering financial losses (e.g., Section 35 misstatement in prospectus).
Criminal liability = penal, aimed at punishment and deterrence (e.g., Section 447 fraud).
'Officer in default' defines who is actually responsible for compliance failures.
Compounding (Section 441) allows settling compoundable offenses via a fee before or after prosecution.
Serious fraud and offenses with mandatory imprisonment combined with other factors may be non-compoundable.
15.importance_reason: This topic forms the foundational enforcement backbone of corporate law and is a permanent fixture in university exams and professional assessments.

16.lecture_title: Statement in Lieu of Prospectus: The Private Route to Public Capital
16.memory_hook: Think of a Statement in Lieu of Prospectus as a quiet disclosure form submitted when a public company decides to skip the grand public invitation dance and quietly secure capital internally.
16.concept_explanation:
When a public limited company is formed, it generally needs to raise capital from the public at large. To do this transparently, it issues a prospectus—a detailed invitation to the public to subscribe for its shares or debentures, laden with financial disclosures and liability safeguards. However, not every public company wishes to go through the expensive and rigorous process of issuing a public prospectus. Sometimes, a company may have enough private connections, promoters, or institutional backers to raise its initial capital privately without inviting subscriptions from the general public.

Under Indian company law, while a public company cannot allot shares without issuing a prospectus, it is granted an alternative if it does not intend to issue a prospectus to the public. Instead of issuing a public invitation, the company must prepare, execute, and file a formal document with the Registrar of Companies (RoC) known as a 'Statement in Lieu of Prospectus'. This document acts as a statutory safety valve, ensuring that even when a company bypasses the public, it still places vital financial and operational facts on public record for regulatory and investor scrutiny.

The Statement in Lieu of Prospectus contains substantially similar information to a regular prospectus, such as details about the directors, minimum subscription, preliminary expenses, and material contracts. By filing this document at least three days before the first allotment of shares, the company satisfies the statutory demand for transparency without launching a full-scale public offering. If a company fails to file this document and proceeds to allot shares, the allotment becomes voidable and attracts severe penal consequences for the company and its defaulting officers.
key_provisions: Section 70 — Prohibits a public company from allotting shares unless a prospectus or a Statement in Lieu of Prospectus has been filed with the Registrar.
Schedule III (Companies Act, 2013 / corresponding provisions of 1956) — Lays down the specific form and detailed contents required to be included in a Statement in Lieu of Prospectus.

case_laws.case_name: Re Indo-China Steam Navigation Co.
case_laws.facts: A public company attempted to bypass statutory disclosure requirements during share distribution by avoiding a formal prospectus, raising questions regarding the mandatory nature of filing alternative disclosure documents.
case_laws.holding: The court held that statutory provisions requiring either a prospectus or a Statement in Lieu of Prospectus are mandatory for public companies, and failure to comply invalidates the foundational integrity of share allotments.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It establishes that statutory disclosure rules cannot be evaded simply because a company chooses to raise funds through restricted or private channels.

case_laws.case_name: Governors of the Peabody Donation Fund v. Sir Lindsay Parkinson & Co.
case_laws.facts: The case examined the extent of statutory duty and public accountability when corporations engage in procedural shortcuts or bypass mandatory filings.
case_laws.holding: Courts emphasized that statutory filing requirements enacted for public protection must be strictly adhered to, and internal arrangements cannot override statutory mandates.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It reinforces the legislative intent behind mandatory disclosure documents like the Statement in Lieu of Prospectus.

16.real_world_example: When a mid-sized infrastructure firm converts from a private limited company to a public limited company to bid for massive government tenders, its founders decide to infuse their own capital and take private equity from venture funds rather than facing the high costs of an Initial Public Offering (IPO). Because it is now a public company but is not issuing shares to the public, it must draft and file a Statement in Lieu of Prospectus with the Registrar of Companies before it can legally allot those shares to the private investors.
16.illustration: Alpha Public Limited Company decides not to issue a prospectus to the public and instead arranges for its promoters to buy all its initial shares. Before making the first allotment of shares to these promoters, Alpha PLC fails to file a Statement in Lieu of Prospectus with the Registrar of Companies. A disgruntled shareholder later challenges the allotment. Legally, the allotment is invalid because Section 70 mandates the filing of either a prospectus or a Statement in Lieu of Prospectus prior to allotment by any public company.
16.quick_answer: A Statement in Lieu of Prospectus is a statutory document that a public limited company must prepare, sign, and file with the Registrar of Companies (RoC) at least three days before making any allotment of shares, if it does not issue a prospectus to the public. Governed broadly under provisions like Section 70 of the Companies Act, this document ensures that transparency and accountability are maintained even when a public company raises capital privately from its promoters or close networks. It contains detailed disclosures regarding company management, property acquisitions, and preliminary expenses. Failure to file this document renders share allotments irregular or voidable, and attracts penalties for the company and defaulting officers.
16.essay_answer:
Introduction
Transparency is the bedrock of corporate regulation. While private companies are shielded from public scrutiny, public companies owe a duty of disclosure to the market and regulatory authorities. However, a public company does not always raise capital through a public offering; it may secure funds privately from promoters, directors, or select institutional investors. To balance corporate flexibility with investor protection, company law provides for a 'Statement in Lieu of Prospectus'.

Nature and Purpose
A Statement in Lieu of Prospectus is a formal document filed by a public company that does not issue a prospectus upon its formation or when it proceeds to allot shares without a public invitation. Its primary objective is to prevent companies from circumventing statutory disclosure norms simply by avoiding a public issue. By forcing the company to place key financial, structural, and contractual details on public record with the Registrar of Companies (RoC), the law ensures that creditors, future investors, and regulators are not left in the dark.

Statutory Requirements and Contents
Under the statutory framework (such as Section 70 of the Companies Act), a public company is strictly prohibited from allotting shares or debentures unless it has registered either a formal prospectus or a duly executed Statement in Lieu of Prospectus. The document must be framed in accordance with prescribed schedules and signed by every person named therein as a director or proposed director. It typically includes disclosures about the minimum subscription, details of vendors, amounts payable for goodwill or property, and particulars of any preliminary expenses incurred.

Legal Consequences of Non-Compliance
Compliance with this requirement is mandatory. If shares are allotted without filing the Statement in Lieu of Prospectus, the transaction suffers from a statutory defect. Courts have consistently held that statutory safeguards designed to protect corporate integrity cannot be bypassed through internal shortcuts. Furthermore, default attracts heavy fines and penalties for the company and every officer in default, reinforcing the gravity of statutory disclosures.

Conclusion
The Statement in Lieu of Prospectus bridges the gap between private capital raising and public company accountability. It ensures that the shield of incorporation as a public entity cannot be abused to escape transparency, safeguarding the interests of all corporate stakeholders.
16.exam_angle: This topic is typically tested in short notes or as a sub-part of a larger essay question on 'Prospectus and Allotment of Shares'. Examiners look for precise references to the statutory requirement of filing the document before allotment and the distinction between a public prospectus and this private alternative. A top-scoring answer clearly distinguishes between companies that issue a prospectus and those that file a statement in lieu.
quick_recap: Applicable only to public companies that do not issue a prospectus to the public.
Must be filed with the Registrar of Companies (RoC) before the first allotment of shares.
Acts as a regulatory safeguard ensuring public transparency even for private capital raising.
Contains details on directors, minimum subscription, vendors, and preliminary expenses.
Failure to file renders share allotments legally defective and invites penalties.
16.importance_reason: It is a standard conceptual topic in Unit II frequently tested in short notes, though less dominant than major prospectus misrepresentation questions.

17.lecture_title: Pre-incorporation Contracts and Legal Status: The Ghost of Contracts Past
17.memory_hook: Think of a pre-incorporation contract as ordering wedding caterers before the bride and groom have even met—the unborn company cannot sign, so the enthusiastic promoter who booked them holds the bill.
17.concept_explanation:
Imagine you want to start a business, but before you can officially register your company with the Registrar of Companies (RoC), you find an incredible commercial office space or negotiate a vital supply deal. You sign the contract in the name of the 'yet-to-be-born' company. Legally, a company is a separate legal entity born only upon the issuance of its Certificate of Incorporation. Before that birth, it has no legal existence, no mind, and no capacity to contract. Consequently, any agreement made on behalf of an unformed company is known as a pre-incorporation or provisional contract.

Under English common law, such contracts were treated as absolute nullities. Because a non-existent principal cannot ratify a contract made by an agent, the company could neither sue nor be sued on it, and the promoter who signed it was personally liable. Indian law has evolved to balance commercial reality with statutory protection. Under the Specific Relief Act, 1963, specific statutory mechanisms allow a company to adopt these contracts post-incorporation if they fall within the terms of incorporation and the company accepts them.

From a practical standpoint, this creates a high-stakes dance for promoters. If the company is never formed, or refuses to adopt the contract after incorporation, the promoter is left holding the bag of personal liability. Conversely, if the third party backs out before incorporation, the promoter may face stranded investments. Therefore, modern corporate practice relies heavily on drafting novation agreements—essentially wiping the slate clean and rewriting the contract directly between the third party and the newly born company—rather than relying solely on post-incorporation adoption.
key_provisions: Section 15(h) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 — Enables the newly incorporated company to enforce a pre-incorporation contract if the contract is warranted by the terms of incorporation and the company has accepted it.

Section 19(e) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 — Allows the other party to enforce a pre-incorporation contract against the newly incorporated company if the company has accepted the contract and communicated such acceptance.
Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Requires lawful consideration and competent parties, which an unformed company strictly lacks.

case_laws.case_name: Kelner v. Baxter
case_laws.facts: Promoters of an intended hotel company signed an agreement to buy wine on behalf of the company before it was incorporated. The company later went into liquidation without paying for the wine, and the suppliers sued the promoters personally.
case_laws.holding: The court held that the promoters were personally liable on the contract because the company did not exist at the time of the contract, and a company cannot ratify a pre-incorporation contract.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It established the bedrock common law principle that a person who signs a contract purporting to act as an agent for a non-existent principal is personally bound by it.

case_laws.case_name: Newborne v. Sensolid Great Britain Ltd.
case_laws.facts: A businessman signed a contract in the name of a company that was in the process of being formed, but the incorporation certificate had not yet been issued. When the buyer breached, the 'company' sued.
case_laws.holding: The court held that neither the company nor the individual could sue on the contract as a company contract, because the company did not exist, and the signature purported to bind a non-existent corporate entity rather than a human agent.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It highlights the critical technical trap in signature execution during the incorporation phase—signing as a company before it exists can result in a completely unenforceable document.

case_laws.case_name: Phonographic Hire Service Ltd. v. Lane
case_laws.facts: The defendant signed an agreement for the hire of jukeboxes on behalf of a company that was yet to be incorporated. The company never came into existence.
case_laws.holding: The court reaffirmed that the promoter is personally liable under such agreements since there is no principal in existence to shoulder the obligation.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It reinforces the absolute nature of promoter liability when corporate birth fails to materialize.

17.real_world_example: Tech startup founders in Bengaluru often lease luxury co-working spaces and hire core engineering talent months before their private limited company receives its CIN (Corporate Identity Number) from the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. If a dispute arises over rent or salaries during that pre-registration window, landlords and employees look directly to the founders' personal savings accounts, because the startup legal entity is technically a ghost.
17.illustration: Aarav signs a lease agreement for an office building on January 1st, writing his signature as 'Director, Apex Tech Solutions Pvt. Ltd.' At that time, Apex Tech has not yet been incorporated; its Certificate of Incorporation is issued only on February 1st. On February 10th, Apex Tech moves in, pays rent for two months, but then defaults. The landlord sues Aarav personally for the balance of the lease. Under Indian law and the Specific Relief Act, Aarav is personally liable unless Apex Tech has entered into a fresh novation agreement with the landlord, because mere post-occupation does not automatically substitute the company for the promoter without clear statutory adoption or novation.
17.quick_answer: Pre-incorporation contracts are agreements made by promoters on behalf of a company before it receives its Certificate of Incorporation. Under common law, a non-existent company cannot contract or ratify agreements, making promoters personally liable (Kelner v. Baxter). However, under Sections 15(h) and 19(e) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a company can adopt these contracts post-incorporation if they are warranted by its incorporation terms and the company accepts them. To avoid personal liability, promoters typically use novation agreements, replacing the provisional contract with a direct contract between the third party and the newly formed company.
17.essay_answer:
Introduction: The journey of a corporate entity from an idea to a legal reality involves a crucial gestation period. During this phase, promoters frequently enter into commercial arrangements—securing leases, hiring key personnel, and acquiring assets—to ensure the business hits the ground running upon incorporation. These agreements are known as pre-incorporation or provisional contracts. This essay examines their legal status, the evolution of promoter liability, and the statutory framework governing them under Indian law.

Legal Status and Common Law Position: At the heart of corporate jurisprudence lies the concept of separate legal entity, established in Salomon v. Salomon & Co. A company comes into legal existence only upon the issuance of the Certificate of Incorporation by the Registrar of Companies. Before this milestone, the company is a legal non-entity; it has no mind, will, or capacity to contract. Consequently, under English common law, pre-incorporation contracts are absolute nullities from the perspective of the unborn company. A non-existent principal cannot appoint an agent, nor can it subsequently ratify a contract made before its birth. In the landmark case of Kelner v. Baxter, the court established that promoters who sign contracts on behalf of an unformed company are personally bound as principals. Similarly, in Newborne v. Sensolid, the court emphasized that improper execution in the name of a non-existent company can render a contract entirely unenforceable by the purported entity.

Indian Statutory Framework: Unlike strict English common law, Indian law provides a statutory cushion through the Specific Relief Act, 1963. Section 15(h) permits a newly incorporated company to enforce a pre-incorporation contract if the contract is warranted by the terms of incorporation and the company has accepted it. Conversely, Section 19(e) allows the third party to enforce the contract against the company if the company has accepted it and communicated such acceptance. Despite these provisions, the primary liability initially rests with the promoter unless a novation occurs.

Promoter Liability and Protection Mechanisms: Promoters walk a tightrope. If the company is never incorporated, or if it repudiates the contract post-incorporation, the promoter bears personal liability. To mitigate this risk, smart promoters avoid signing directly as corporate agents. Instead, they utilize 'novation agreements'—tripartite contracts where the third party, the promoter, and the newly incorporated company agree to extinguish the old promoter-led contract and substitute it with a direct obligation binding solely on the company. Alternatively, clauses can be inserted stating that the promoter's liability ceases entirely once the company adopts the contract.

Conclusion: Pre-incorporation contracts bridge the gap between commercial urgency and corporate formality. While Indian statutory law under the Specific Relief Act provides a pathway for companies to adopt these bargains, the foundational rule remains that promoters bear personal risk until corporate birth is complete and formal novation or adoption occurs. Thorough drafting and precise legal navigation remain the ultimate safeguards for entrepreneurial ambition.
17.exam_angle: Examiners love testing this topic through practical problem questions where a promoter signs a lease or purchases machinery before incorporation and the company later refuses to pay. To score top marks, you must distinguish between the rigid common law position (personal promoter liability, no ratification) and the Indian statutory position under Sections 15(h) and 19(e) of the Specific Relief Act, while mentioning novation as the practical solution.
quick_recap: A company has no legal existence before the Certificate of Incorporation is issued.
Common law rule: A non-existent principal cannot ratify contracts (Kelner v. Baxter).
Promoters are personally liable for pre-incorporation contracts by default.
Section 15(h) and 19(e) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 allow the company to adopt and enforce these contracts post-incorporation.
Novation is the safest commercial method to transfer liability from the promoter to the company.
17.importance_reason: Pre-incorporation contracts appear frequently in both short-answer and long-essay sections of University exams because they test the fundamental mechanics of separate legal personality and agency law.

18.lecture_title: Company Law Unit II: The Anatomy of Membership — How You Become a Shareholder in an Indian Company
18.memory_hook: Think of becoming a member like getting married: simply agreeing to it or having someone talk about it isn't enough; your name must be officially registered in the sacred book (the Register of Members) to make the union legally binding.
18.concept_explanation:
In corporate law, the distinction between a 'shareholder' and a 'member' is often blurred in casual conversation, but in the eyes of the Companies Act, 2013, they are two sides of the same coin with distinct legal nuances. While every person whose name is entered in the Register of Members (ROM) is a member, a person who merely holds a share certificate transferred in blank without registration in the company's books is not yet a member. Membership is the status acquired by a person who holds a share and whose name is duly entered in the register of members maintained by the company under Section 88, or whose name is entered as a beneficial owner in the records of a depository under the Depositories Act, 1996.

First principles dictate that to become a member, two fundamental conditions must concurrently be satisfied: first, there must be an agreement to become a member (consent, application, or transfer), and second, the company must enter the applicant's name into the Register of Members. Without the entry in the register, the rights and liabilities of a member do not attach to the individual. This dual requirement protects both the company—knowing precisely who its owners are for voting and dividend purposes—and the investor, ensuring they are not fraudulently thrust into corporate liabilities without formal acknowledgment.

Capacity to become a member is another crucial pillar. Generally, any person competent to contract under Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, can become a member of a company. Minors, being incompetent to contract, cannot enter into a contract to take shares. Therefore, an allotment of shares to a minor is void ab initio, and the minor's name cannot be placed on the register. However, shares can be validly held by a minor if they are fully paid-up and acquired by way of transfer or inheritance through a lawful guardian, provided no further liability or call money attaches to those shares. Similarly, an insolvent can remain a member until their name is removed, but the official assignee or receiver exercises all voting and dividend rights.

Finally, membership can cease through various modes: by transfer of shares where the transferee's name replaces the transferor's, by forfeiture or surrender of shares, by the death or insolvency of the member (where legal representatives step in without becoming members themselves unless registered), by the winding up of the company, or by redemption of redeemable preference shares. Understanding this lifecycle of membership is essential for navigating corporate governance, liability enforcement, and shareholder democracy under Indian company law.
key_provisions: Section 2(55) — Defines 'member' of a company.
Section 88 — Requires every company to maintain a Register of Members.
Section 89 — Mandates declaration in respect of beneficial interest in any shares.
Section 90 — Register of significant beneficial owners in a company.
Section 112/113 — Representation of bodies corporate and President/Governors at meetings.

case_laws.case_name: Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT
case_laws.facts: The assessee company claimed dividend income on shares held by it, though its name was not entered in the register of members of the issuing companies, arguing it was the beneficial owner holding transfer deeds.
case_laws.holding: The Supreme Court held that only the person whose name is entered in the register of members is a 'member' of the company for all statutory purposes, regardless of who holds the beneficial interest or share certificates.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It establishes the absolute primacy of the Register of Members in determining legal membership and rights in Indian company law.

case_laws.case_name: Balwant Singh v. Mahanagar Co-operative Bank
case_laws.facts: Disputes arose regarding whether persons whose names were irregularly entered or who lacked valid share application processes could exercise voting rights as members.
case_laws.holding: The court reiterated that entry in the register of members is mandatory, and mere possession of share scrips without formal registration does not confer membership status.
case_laws.why_it_matters: Reinforces the dual test of agreement plus registration for valid membership.

case_laws.case_name: Official Liquidator, Mgt. v. Dayanand
case_laws.facts: Employees were allotted shares as part of a scheme, but questions arose regarding whether they became valid members liable as contributories upon the company's winding up.
case_laws.holding: The court emphasized that once the statutory formalities of application, allotment, and entry in the register are complete, membership status crystallizes, attracting liabilities upon liquidation.
case_laws.why_it_matters: Clarifies the moment of crystallization of membership liabilities during company winding up.

18.real_world_example: In contemporary capital markets, when retail investors buy shares on platforms like Zerodha or Groww, their shares are held in dematerialized (demat) form through depositories like NSDL or CDSL. Under Section 2(55)(iii) of the Companies Act, 2013, the depository is recorded as the registered owner in the company's register, but the retail investor is recorded as the 'beneficial owner' in the depository's records. This modern statutory fiction allows millions of daily stock traders to enjoy full member rights—such as voting at Annual General Meetings and receiving dividends—without every single retail investor's name having to be manually entered into the company's physical ledger.
18.illustration: Aakash applies for 500 shares in Zeta Pharmaceuticals Ltd. and pays the application money. The company allots the shares and dispatches the share certificates to Aakash, but due to an administrative oversight, the company's secretarial department forgets to enter Aakash's name into the Register of Members. Two months later, Zeta Pharmaceuticals goes into liquidation, and the liquidator attempts to place Aakash's name on the list of contributories for unpaid calls. Aakash argues he is not a member because his name is never in the register. Applying the dual test under Section 2(55), Aakash succeeds: because entry in the register is a mandatory prerequisite alongside the agreement/allotment, he is not legally a member and escapes contributory liability.
18.quick_answer: Under Section 2(55) of the Companies Act, 2013, a 'member' of a company is defined as: (a) a subscriber to the memorandum of association who is deemed to have agreed to become a member, (b) every other person who agrees in writing to become a member and whose name is entered in the register of members, and (c) every person holding shares in dematerialized form and whose name is recorded as a beneficial owner with a depository. The two essential requisites for membership are a valid contract/agreement to become a member and the entry of the person's name in the Register of Members (ROM). A shareholder is someone who holds shares, but a member is someone whose name is officially registered. Minors and insolvents have restricted capacities regarding membership. Membership can be acquired via subscription, application and allotment, transfer, or transmission, and ceases via transfer, forfeiture, surrender, or winding up.
18.essay_answer:
Introduction: In corporate jurisprudence, the cornerstone of corporate democracy and ownership is the concept of 'membership'. While commercial parlance often uses 'shareholder' and 'member' interchangeably, the Companies Act, 2013, draws subtle yet profound legal boundaries between the two. Understanding who constitutes a member is vital not only for determining voting rights, dividend entitlements, and meeting requisitions but also for establishing liability during corporate distress and liquidation.

Statutory Definition and Requisites: Section 2(55) of the Companies Act, 2013, exhaustively defines a member. It encompasses three distinct categories: first, subscribers to the memorandum of association, who automatically become members upon incorporation without needing a separate application or registration; second, any person who agrees in writing to become a member and whose name is entered in the company's Register of Members; and third, beneficial owners whose names are recorded with a depository under the Depositories Act, 1996. From this statutory architecture, two cumulative conditions emerge: a valid agreement to become a member and the ministerial entry of the name in the Register of Members (maintained under Section 88). As established in landmark jurisprudence like Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT, mere holding of share certificates or blank transfer deeds does not confer membership status until the company formally registers the transfer.

Modes of Acquiring Membership: Membership can be acquired through several legally recognized modes: 1. Subscription: Subscribers to the Memorandum become members ipso facto upon incorporation. 2. Application and Allotment: An ordinary investor applies for shares; when the board accepts the application and allots shares, a binding contract is formed, leading to registration. 3. Transfer of Shares: An existing member transfers their shares to an outsider, requiring the execution of a transfer deed and subsequent registration by the company. 4. Transmission of Shares: Operation of law, such as upon the death, insanity, or insolvency of a member, where legal representatives acquire rights without formal fresh application, though they must elect whether to become registered members. 5. Acquiring shares through a Depository: Demat holdings where the depository acts as the registered owner and the investor is the beneficial owner.

Capacity of Parties: To become a member, an individual must possess contractual capacity under the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Minors lack capacity; hence, an allotment of partly paid shares to a minor is void. However, fully paid-up shares can be held by a guardian on behalf of a minor. Joint holders can become members, with their rights and liabilities governed by the articles of association, where the order of names in the register determines who receives notices and voting primacy. Corporate bodies can also become members by passing a board resolution under Section 112.

Termination of Membership: Membership ceases when an individual's name is removed from the register of members. This occurs via transfer of shares, forfeiture, surrender, redemption of preference shares, disclaimer of onerous property by an insolvent's assignee, death (though estate liability remains), or the complete winding up and dissolution of the company.

Conclusion: Membership is the legal bridge connecting an investor to the corporate entity. It defines the contours of corporate governance, granting individuals the power to steer corporate policy while binding them to statutory obligations. A precise grasp of Section 2(55) and the mechanics of the Register of Members ensures that corporate rights and liabilities are accurately channeled to the rightful owners.
18.exam_angle: Examiners frequently test this topic through direct 10-15 mark essay questions ("Define member and explain the modes of acquiring and terminating membership") or short problem-based queries involving minors or unregistered transfers. To score top marks, explicitly distinguish between a 'shareholder' and a 'member' using Section 2(55) and weave in the mandatory dual requirement of agreement plus registration supported by case law like Howrah Trading.
quick_recap: Section 2(55) defines a member: subscriber, registered agreement holder, or beneficial owner in demat.
Dual test for membership: Valid agreement + Entry in the Register of Members (ROM).
Shareholder vs. Member: All members are shareholders (usually), but not all shareholders are members until registered.
Minors cannot contract for partly paid shares, but can hold fully paid shares via guardians.
Modes of acquisition: Subscription, Allotment, Transfer, Transmission, and Depository holding.
Cessation occurs via transfer, forfeiture, surrender, death, or company winding up.
18.importance_reason: Membership forms the bedrock of corporate democracy and liability, making it a recurring favorite for both short notes and major essay questions in University exams.

19.topic: Borrowing Powers and Ultra Vires Borrowing
19.lecture_title: Borrowing Powers and Ultra Vires Borrowing in Company Law
19.memory_hook: A company can stretch its borrowing arm only as far as its Memorandum allows, but if it reaches beyond the ultra vires horizon, the lender's money vanishes into thin air without creating a single legal debt.
19.concept_explanation:
A company, being an artificial legal person created by process of law, does not possess inherent natural capacities like a human being. Its existence is circumscribed by its founding documents—specifically the Memorandum of Association (MoA) and the Articles of Association (AoA). When a company needs funds to run its business, it must possess the legal capacity or 'power' to borrow money. This power is usually expressly stated in the objects or incidental powers clause of the MoA, or it can be implied if the company is a trading company whose ordinary course of business necessitates raising capital or taking credit.

However, problems arise when a company borrows beyond its authorized limits or when the borrowing falls entirely outside the scope of objects permitted by its MoA. This is known as 'Ultra Vires Borrowing'. In Latin, 'ultra' means beyond and 'vires' means powers. When a company borrows beyond the limits set by the shareholders in the AoA (such as restricting borrowing to the amount of paid-up capital without a board resolution), it is an intra vires act of the company (because the company as a whole has borrowing powers) but ultra vires the directors. Such internal irregularities can often be cured or ratified by shareholders, and protected by the indoor management rule.

Conversely, when a borrowing is completely outside the objects clause of the MoA, it is ultra vires the company itself. Such a transaction is void ab initio—meaning it is a complete nullity from the very beginning. Because the contract is void, no legal debt is created, the lender cannot sue the company for repayment on the contract, and the company cannot ratify it even if every single shareholder agrees. The money does not become company property in the true sense, triggering specific equitable remedies for the lender to trace and recover their funds.

To mitigate the harsh consequences for innocent lenders, equity developed protective remedies. If the borrowed money has not been spent and is still identifiable in a separate bank account, the lender can obtain an injunction to restrain the company from parting with it and seek a tracing order. Furthermore, if the company used the ultra vires borrowed funds to pay off its lawful debts, the lender is subrogated to the rights of those paid-off creditors, stepping into their shoes to the extent the funds were so applied. Understanding this balance between strict corporate capacity and equitable relief forms the core of this lecture.
key_provisions: Section 2(87) — defines subsidiary companies and impacts group borrowing calculations
Section 179(3)(d) — mandates that the Board of Directors must exercise its power to borrow monies by means of resolutions passed at meetings of the Board
Section 180 — restricts the powers of the Board by requiring ordinary or special shareholder resolutions for borrowing beyond paid-up capital and free reserves
Section 6 — gives overriding effect to the Companies Act, 2013 over the memorandum and articles

case_laws.case_name: Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd. v. Riche
case_laws.facts: The company's memorandum stated its objects were to make and sell railway plant and carriages. The directors entered into a contract to finance the construction of a railway in Belgium, which the majority of shareholders later attempted to ratify.
case_laws.holding: The House of Lords held that the contract was ultra vires the company and therefore completely void. Even a unanimous ratification by shareholders could not make it valid.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It established the bedrock principle that a company's capacity is strictly limited to the objects set out in its Memorandum of Association, and ultra vires contracts are void ab initio.

case_laws.case_name: In re Jon Beauforte (London) Ltd.
case_laws.facts: A company whose memorandum authorized it to carry on the business of tailors sought to manufactureveneered panels. It borrowed money from its bank specifically to pay for builders and materials for this new, unauthorized business, and the bank was aware of the intended use.
case_laws.holding: The court held that the borrowings were ultra vires the company. Since the bank knew the money was being borrowed for an ultra vires purpose, the bank could not prove in the liquidation as a creditor for money lent.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It illustrates how lender knowledge and the direct application of funds to ultra vires objects destroys the lender's ordinary contractual remedies, though subrogation saved part of the claim where funds paid valid debts.

19.real_world_example: When large infrastructure conglomerates or shadow banking companies face sudden liquidity crunches, their corporate treasuries often attempt to raise emergency debt through complex commercial paper or inter-corporate deposits. If a corporate borrower's constitutional documents do not permit engaging in speculative financial layering or lending outside its core manufacturing sector, institutional lenders conduct intense due diligence. If the borrowing exceeds limits set under Section 180 without shareholder approval, the debt covenants are triggered, forcing board restructuring or immediate loan recalls to prevent ultra vires fallout.
19.illustration: XYZ Engineering Ltd. has a Memorandum of Association that restricts its borrowing power to a maximum ceiling of Rs. 10 Crores. The Articles of Association require any borrowing above Rs. 5 Crores to be approved by a special resolution of shareholders. Without passing any resolution, the Managing Director approaches ABC Bank and borrows Rs. 12 Crores. Later, the company refuses to repay, claiming the borrowing is ultra vires. Analysis: The borrowing of Rs. 10 Crores authorized by the MoA is an intra vires act of the company, but the excess Rs. 2 Crores is ultra vires the company's objects/powers limit. Furthermore, the failure to obtain the special resolution makes the entire loan an internal irregularity governed by the indoor management rule for the first Rs. 10 crores, but the excess Rs. 2 Crores that breaches the absolute limit in the MoA remains void, though the company is bound up to its constitutional ceiling.
19.quick_answer: Borrowing powers refer to a company's legal authority to raise loans, which must be authorized by its Memorandum and Articles of Association. Under Section 179(3)(d) of the Companies Act, 2013, the board exercises this power via board resolutions, subject to the limits in Section 180 requiring shareholder approval. Ultra vires borrowing occurs when a loan falls outside the company's objects clause in the MoA (ultra vires the company) or exceeds internal board limits (ultra vires the directors). Borrowing ultra vires the company is completely void ab initio; no debt is created, and the lender cannot sue on the contract. However, equity protects lenders through tracing unspent funds or subrogation where money paid off lawful debts. Borrowing ultra vires the directors is merely an internal irregularity that can be ratified by shareholders.
19.essay_answer:
Introduction: The ability to raise capital through debt is the lifeblood of modern corporate enterprise. However, unlike a natural person, a registered company does not possess an inherent, unlimited capacity to borrow money. Its borrowing powers are strictly circumscribed by its foundational constitutional documents—the Memorandum of Association (MoA) and the Articles of Association (AoA)—alongside statutory frameworks like the Companies Act, 2013. When a company crosses these legal frontiers, the phenomenon of 'Ultra Vires Borrowing' arises, presenting complex legal tensions between corporate governance safeguards and commercial equity.

Statutory Framework and Board Powers: Under Section 179(3)(d) of the Companies Act, 2013, the power to borrow monies and invest funds is vested squarely in the Board of Directors, exercisable only through resolutions passed at board meetings. However, this power is not absolute. Section 180 imposes statutory fetters, prohibiting the Board from borrowing monies exceeding the aggregate of the company's paid-up share capital, free reserves, and securities premium (apart from temporary loans obtained from the company's bankers in the ordinary course of business) without prior approval of shareholders by way of a special resolution. If the board borrows in violation of Section 180 without shareholder consent, the act is ultra vires the directors.

Distinction Between Ultra Vires the Company and Ultra Vires the Directors: Legal theory draws a sharp line between acts that are ultra vires the company and those that are ultra vires the directors. When a borrowing violates the objects clause of the MoA, it is ultra vires the company itself. Grounded in the classic House of Lords ruling in Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd. v. Riche, such a transaction is void ab initio. It creates no debtor-creditor relationship, cannot be ratified even by unanimous shareholder consent, and bars the lender from suing for recovery under contract. Conversely, if the company possesses the overarching power to borrow under its MoA, but the directors exceed their internal authority under the AoA or fail to pass required resolutions, it is ultra vires the directors. This constitutes an internal irregularity. Under the rule in Royal British Bank v. Turquand (Indoor Management Rule), innocent third-party lenders are entitled to assume that internal procedural requirements have been duly complied with.

Equitable Remedies for Lenders: Because treating ultra vires loans as entirely irrecoverable frequently results in unjust enrichment of the company at the expense of innocent lenders, courts of equity have carved out specific relief mechanisms. First, if the borrowed funds remain identifiable and unspent in a segregated bank account, the lender can trace the money and obtain an injunction preventing the company from using it. Second, under the doctrine of subrogation, if the ultra vires borrowed money was utilized by the company to discharge its valid, lawful pre-existing debts, the lender is subrogated to the rights of those paid-off creditors. The lender steps into their shoes, permitting recovery to that exact extent, though without claiming the contractual interest rate.

Conclusion: Borrowing powers and their ultra vires limitations serve as vital checks protecting shareholders and creditors against reckless corporate expansion outside authorized domains. While strict application of the ultra vires doctrine prevents companies from straying into unauthorized ventures, equitable doctrines ensure that commerce is not paralyzed by absolute forfeiture. A balanced harmony between statutory compliance under the Companies Act, 2013 and equitable tracing preserves both corporate integrity and commercial fairness.
19.exam_angle: Examiners frequently test this topic through problem-based long-form essay questions where a company exceeds its MoA borrowing limits or violates Section 180. To score top marks, clearly distinguish between 'ultra vires the company' (void, no debt) and 'ultra vires the directors' (voidable/irregular, curable by shareholders), while weaving in equitable remedies like subrogation and tracing.
quick_recap: Company borrowing power must originate in the MoA and be exercised by directors under Section 179(3)(d).
Section 180 restricts board borrowing beyond paid-up capital and free reserves without a special resolution.
Ultra vires the company means outside the objects clause; the contract is void ab initio.
Ultra vires the directors is an internal irregularity protected by the indoor management rule.
Equitable remedies like tracing unspent funds and subrogation save innocent lenders from total loss.
